Positive random-environment path-weight martingale (Zt​=Eξ​∏j=1t​(1+εh(j,ξj​)))

Words: 193 Articles: 2
Martingale OurBigBook.com
Let ξ be a random walk, independent of centered, independent time-space signs h, and let 0<ε<1. Averaging over the walk gives a positive martingale in the environment filtration: each new time layer has conditional mean-one weight. Hence EZt​=1 and the martingale convergence theorem gives a finite nonnegative almost-sure limit. Preserving its mean requires an additional condition such as bounded second moments; positivity of finite-time weights alone does not suffice.

Tail event for a vanishing positive path-weight limit

Words: 73
Positive random-environment path-weight martingale OurBigBook.com
Delete the first m environment factors from the path-weight expectation and call the result ZT(m)​. Pointwise, (1−ε)mZT(m)​≤ZT​≤(1+ε)mZT(m)​. Thus {liminfT​ZT​=0} equals {liminfT​ZT(m)​=0} and belongs to every future-time environment sigma-algebra. The Kolmogorov zero-one law makes its probability zero or one. If the nonnegative martingale limit has mean one, the probability cannot be one, so its limit is strictly positive almost surely. The pointwise comparison establishes a genuine tail event, rather than merely invariance outside an unspecified exceptional set.

Collision-count second moment for independent path weights (EZt2​=Eξ(1),ξ(2)​(1+ε2)It​)

Words: 57
Positive random-environment path-weight martingale OurBigBook.com
Here It​=∑j=1t​1{ξj(1)​=ξj(2)​}​ counts simultaneous collisions of two independent walks. A shared environment sign contributes E(1+εh)2=1+ε2; distinct signs contribute one. If the difference walk returns to zero with probability ρ<1, its total number of positive-time returns has law P(I∞​=k)=(1−ρ)ρk. Therefore the second moments are bounded by (1−ρ)/(1−ρ(1+ε2)) whenever ρ(1+ε2)<1. Convergence in L2 then preserves the limit's mean one.

eθh−1−θh≤2(1−θc/3)θ2h2​(∣h∣≤c)
(1)

Ville inequality (Pr(supt​Mt​≥a)≤EM0​/a)

Words: 59
Martingale OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative martingale, the displayed maximal probability bound follows by stopping at the first crossing of a. The stopped expectation is at most its initial expectation, and on the crossing event its value is at least a. Bound the stopping time first and pass to the limit using nonnegativity. This form is useful for the Poisson maximal concentration bound.

Finite voter-model consensus probability

Words: 81
Martingale OurBigBook.com
In a finite population that repeatedly lets one uniformly chosen individual copy a uniformly chosen distinct individual, the fraction of either type is a bounded martingale. Conditional probabilities of an increase and decrease coincide. Absorption at one of the two unanimous states occurs almost surely, since from every state there is a uniformly positive probability of reaching unanimity in a fixed finite block of updates. Bounded convergence implies that the probability of eventual unanimity of one type equals its initial fraction.

Unchanging betting probability under sampling without replacement (q(r,b)=r(r−1)/[(r+b)(r+b−1)])

Words: 84
Martingale OurBigBook.com
In a uniformly shuffled deck with r red and b black cards remaining, the conditional probability that the next two are red is q(r,b). If at least three cards remain, q(r,b) is the weighted average of q(r−1,b) and q(r,b−1) after one reveal. Hence these probabilities form a bounded martingale until only two cards remain. Any adapted choice of exactly one betting time before that deadline has the same winning probability by bounded optional stopping. Waiting creates no advantage when a bet must eventually be made.

Nonnegative martingale (Mn​≥0)

Words: 42
Martingale OurBigBook.com
A nonnegative martingale takes nonnegative values almost surely at each time. In discrete time its expectations are constant, so it is bounded in L1 and the martingale convergence theorem gives a finite integrable almost sure limit. Its expectations need not converge to the expectation of that limit; uniform integrability is needed for convergence in L1.

Doob exposure martingale (Mi​=E[f∣Z1​,…,Zi​])

Words: 56
Martingale OurBigBook.com
Expose independent coordinates successively and take the conditional mean of a function after each exposure. These conditional means form a martingale from Ef to f. A coordinate oscillation bound ci​ gives a conditional interval of length ci​ for the corresponding increment, by coupling the unexposed coordinates. Applying the Hoeffding lemma to these conditional ranges proves the McDiarmid inequality.

Rare-jump martingale divergence (Xn​=∑k=1n​(1−2kYk​))

Words: 53
Martingale OurBigBook.com
A martingale can diverge to +∞ almost surely when its increments are finite but not uniformly bounded. For independent Bernoulli random variables with P(Yn​=1)=2−n,
Xn​=∑k=1n​(1−2kYk​)
(2)
has centered integrable increments. The First Borel-Cantelli lemma makes the rare negative jumps occur only finitely often, after which every increment equals one. The expectation remains zero at every finite time despite this pathwise divergence.

Characterization of a martingale by bounded continuous-time stopped expectations (EXT​=EX0​)

Words: 55
Martingale OurBigBook.com
An integrable adapted process is a martingale if all its values at bounded stopping times are integrable with the same expectation as X0​. For the converse, compare deterministic t with U=s1A​+t1Ac​, where s<t and A∈Fs​. The resulting identity E[(Xt​−Xs​)1A​]=0 is precisely the defining test for conditional expectation. In the forward direction, use the optional stopping theorem for a càdlàg martingale under the usual conditions for a filtration.

Azuma's inequality (P(MN​−M0​≤−t)≤e−t2/(2∑i​ci2​))

Words: 104 Articles: 1
Martingale OurBigBook.com
If a martingale has increments with ∣Mi​−Mi−1​∣≤ci​ almost surely for deterministic ci​, then each one-sided deviation of magnitude t>0 from M0​ has probability at most exp(−t2/(2∑i​ci2​)). If all ci​ vanish, the martingale is constant. The inequality gives concentration from bounded increments without requiring independent increments.

Two-sided Azuma-Hoeffding inequality (P(∣Mn​−M0​∣≥x)≤2e−x2/(2∑k=1n​ck2​))

Words: 58
Azuma's inequality OurBigBook.com
For deterministic bounds ∣Mk​−Mk−1​∣≤ck​, the conditional mean-zero increment has exponential moment at most eθ2ck2​/2. Iteration, the Markov inequality and optimization at θ=x/∑ck2​ give each one-sided tail, and the union bound gives the displayed inequality. The factor two in the exponent denominator cannot be omitted: a single symmetric increment of size one has absolute deviation one with probability one.

Martingale increments obstruct finite convergence

Words: 37
Martingale OurBigBook.com
If a real sequence converges finitely, its successive increments tend to zero. A martingale whose increments stay bounded away from zero on every sample path cannot have a finite almost-sure limit, regardless of its zero conditional mean increments.

Absorption at zero of a nonnegative martingale (Mn​=0(n≥T0​))

Words: 174 Articles: 2
Martingale OurBigBook.com
Once a nonnegative martingale hits zero, it stays zero almost surely. Conditional expectation on {Mn​=0} gives E[Mn+1​1{Mn​=0}​]=0; nonnegativity forces the next value to vanish there. A countable intersection makes these assertions simultaneous for all times, proving absorption at the first zero.

Absorption-time bound from conditional variance and overshoot (E(T∧TR​)≤(τR−1)/σ2)

Words: 134 Articles: 1
Absorption at zero of a nonnegative martingale OurBigBook.com
Let a nonnegative martingale start at one, let T be its first zero, and let TR​ be its first hit of [R,∞). Suppose E[(Mn+1​−Mn​)2∣Fn​]≥σ21{T>n}​ and MTR​​≤τR on finite hits, for thresholds R≥1. Then MT∧TR​∧n2​−σ2(T∧TR​∧n) is a submartingale. The bounded stopped values have mean one, so their second moment is at most τR. Consequently E(T∧TR​)≤(τR−1)/σ2. For τ≥1 this implies the weaker bound τ2R/σ2. The threshold restriction prevents an impossible overshoot requirement below the starting value.

Square-root tail bound for martingale absorption (P(T>n)≤2τ/(σn​))

Absorption-time bound from conditional variance and overshoot OurBigBook.com
Under the conditional-variance and overshoot assumptions of the absorption-time bound from conditional variance and overshoot, P(T>n)≤2τ/(σn​). Bound the probability by P(TR​<∞)+E(T∧TR​)/n and optimize 1/R+τ2R/(σ2n). If the resulting bound is below one, its minimizing threshold is greater than one; otherwise the probability bound is trivial.

Martingale difference sequence (E[Dn​∣Fn−1​]=0)

Words: 131 Articles: 2
Martingale OurBigBook.com
A martingale difference sequence is an adapted sequence of integrable random variables Dn​, n≥1, with E[Dn​∣Fn−1​]=0. Its partial sums are a martingale, and martingale increments give such sequences. If the differences are square-integrable, they are uncorrelated random variables: for j<k, conditioning on Fk−1​ gives EDj​Dk​=0.

Martingale difference (E(Dj​∣Fj−1​)=0)

Words: 34
Martingale difference sequence OurBigBook.com
A time-indexed increment Dj​ with E(Dj​∣Fj−1​)=0 is a martingale difference relative to its history. Square-integrable differences at different indices are orthogonal, allowing their conditional variances to accumulate. They need not be independent.

Strong law for martingales with bounded increments (Mn​/n→0 a.s.)

Words: 45
Martingale difference sequence OurBigBook.com
If a martingale has increments bounded by a single deterministic constant, then Mn​/n→0 almost surely. Its increments form a uniformly L2-bounded martingale difference sequence; apply the strong law for uniformly L2-bounded uncorrelated random variables to their partial sums and note M0​/n→0. No square-integrability of the initial value is needed beyond the usual martingale integrability.

Dyadic slope martingale (Gn​(t)=2n(f((k+1)2−n)−f(k2−n)))

Words: 84
Martingale OurBigBook.com
For a real continuous function f on [0,1], let Gn​ be its secant slope on each length-2−n dyadic cell. Regard ([0,1],B,dt) as a probability space and use the filtration of half-open dyadic cells with the endpoint {1} as a separate null cell. The mean of the two child slopes equals the parent slope, so (Gn​) is a martingale. Its integral gives the linear interpolation of f on that grid. If f is Lipschitz continuous, these slopes are bounded by its Lipschitz constant; the Lp martingale convergence theorem then supplies a bounded integral density for f.

Words: 24
Martingale OurBigBook.com
For fair independent and identically distributed random variables ξj​ with the Bernoulli distribution, Mn​=2n1{ξ1​=⋯=ξn​=1}​ is a nonnegative martingale. It has almost sure convergence to zero but EMn​=1, so it lacks convergence in L1.

Positive martingale majorant of an L1-bounded submartingale (Mn​=limp→∞​E[Xp+​∣Fn​])

Words: 65
Submartingale OurBigBook.com
For a submartingale with supn​E∣Xn​∣=C<∞, its positive part is a submartingale by the conditional Jensen inequality. Thus the displayed conditional expectations increase in p. Their limits are finite almost surely and have expectations at most C, by the monotone convergence theorem. Conditional monotone convergence and the tower property of conditional expectation give E[Mn+1​∣Fn​]=Mn​. Moreover Mn​≥Xn+​. Consequently Yn​=Mn​−Xn​ is a nonnegative supermartingale, supn​EYn​≤2C, and X=M−Y. The resulting martingale need not have uniform integrability.

Doob-Meyer decomposition theorem (X=M+A)

Words: 57
Submartingale OurBigBook.com
Under the usual filtration conditions, a càdlàg submartingale of Class D on a finite horizon has a unique decomposition into a uniformly integrable martingale and a predictable integrable nondecreasing process starting at zero. A general continuous semimartingale decomposition instead allows an arbitrary continuous finite-variation drift. A convex function of a semimartingale need not be a submartingale when that drift has unrestricted sign.

Truncated layer-cake proof of the L2 maximal inequality (∥Mt​∥2​≤2∥Xt​∥2​)

Words: 61
Doob maximal inequality for a nonnegative submartingale OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative submartingale with maximum Mt​, the first-moment maximal estimate is λP(Mt​≥λ)≤E[Xt​1{Mt​≥λ}​]. Integrate 2λ times the tail probability only up to R, obtaining E(Mt​∧R)2≤2E[Xt​(Mt​∧R)]. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives ∥Mt​∧R∥2​≤2∥Xt​∥2​, and monotone convergence gives the result as R→∞. Truncation avoids assuming beforehand that the maximum has a finite second moment.

One-sided martingale maximal inequality (P(maxk≤n​Mk​≥x)≤V/(V+x2))

Words: 52
Doob maximal inequality for a nonnegative submartingale OurBigBook.com
For a square-integrable martingale with M0​=0 and V=EMn2​, apply the Doob maximal inequality to (Mk​+c)2 for c≥0. An upper crossing of x implies a square crossing of (x+c)2, giving (V+c2)/(x+c)2. Minimization at c=V/x gives the displayed bound. A one-step martingale taking x with probability V/(V+x2) and −V/x otherwise attains equality when V>0.

Kolmogorov maximal inequality (P(maxk≤n​∣Sk​∣≥x)≤x−2∑j=1n​Eξj2​)

Words: 42
Doob maximal inequality for a nonnegative submartingale OurBigBook.com
For independent zero-mean square-integrable increments, their partial sums form a martingale, and their squares form a nonnegative submartingale. Apply the Doob maximal inequality to the squared process at threshold x2. Independence and zero means make its terminal second moment the sum of the increment variances. Identical distributions are not required.

One-sided maximal inequality for a centered square-integrable martingale (P(maxk≤n​Mk​≥λ)≤v/(λ2+v))

Words: 49
Doob maximal inequality for a nonnegative submartingale OurBigBook.com
For a centered square-integrable martingale with v=EMn2​ and λ>0, apply the Doob maximal inequality for a nonnegative submartingale to (Mk​+c)2 for c≥0. Conditional Jensen inequality gives the submartingale property, and crossing λ forces its square above (λ+c)2. The bound (v+c2)/(λ+c)2 is minimized by c=v/λ. This extends the Cantelli inequality from one random variable to a martingale maximum, without requiring independent increments.

Words: 25
Predictable sigma-algebra OurBigBook.com
Every deterministic càdlàg function is Borel measurable in time. Since the predictable sigma-algebra contains every set Ω×A with A Borel, the corresponding deterministic process is predictable.

Doob decomposition theorem

Words: 138 Articles: 2
Martingale OurBigBook.com
Every integrable discrete-time supermartingale has the form V=M−A, where M is a martingale and A is predictable, integrable, nondecreasing, and starts at zero.
More generally, an integrable adapted process Xn​ decomposes as Xn​=Mn​+An​ with A0​=0 and An​−An−1​=E[Xn​−Xn−1​∣Fn−1​]. For a supermartingale this drift is nonincreasing, so writing it as −A yields the nondecreasing convention above.

Strong law for submartingales with bounded increments (liminfn​Yn​/n≥0 a.s.)

Words: 33
Doob decomposition theorem OurBigBook.com
If a submartingale has uniformly bounded increments, then liminfn​Yn​/n≥0 almost surely. In its Doob decomposition in discrete time, the predictable compensator is nondecreasing, while the martingale part has bounded increments. The strong law for martingales with bounded increments makes the latter negligible on the linear scale.

Doob decomposition of an adapted integrable process

Words: 47
Doob decomposition theorem OurBigBook.com
Every adapted integrable process X has a unique decomposition X=M+A, where M is a martingale, A0​=0, and A is predictable. Its increments are
An+1​−An​=E[Xn+1​−Xn​∣Fn​].
(45)
For a supermartingale these increments are nonpositive; changing the sign of A gives the usual nondecreasing compensator convention.

Snell envelope

Words: 614 Articles: 10
Martingale OurBigBook.com
The finite-horizon Snell envelope of rewards Zn​ is defined backward by VN​=ZN​ and Vn​=max{Zn​,E[Vn+1​∣Fn​]}. It is the least supermartingale dominating Z.

Snell envelope of a multiplicative process (Ut​=Yt​ct​)

Words: 103
Snell envelope OurBigBook.com
Let Yt​=Y0​∏j=1t​Zj​, where Y0​>0 is deterministic and the positive factors are independent and integrable. Use the natural filtration. Its finite-horizon Snell envelope is
Ut​=Yt​ct​,cT​=1,ct​=max{1,ct+1​EZt+1​}.
(46)
Indeed, backward induction and independence of random variables give E[Ut+1​∣Ft​]=Yt​ct+1​EZt+1​; take the maximum with immediate exercise Yt​. The constants are finite and at least one. Equivalently, ct​ is the maximum of 1 and the successive products ∏j=t+1u​EZj​ for t<u≤T. If the factors have a common mean λ>1, waiting until maturity is optimal and ct​=λT−t. Integrability and independence of random variables from the current information are essential to the finite deterministic coefficient conclusion.

Optimal stopping (supτ​E[Zτ​])

Words: 405 Articles: 5
Snell envelope OurBigBook.com
Choosing a stopping time to maximize an expected reward. For an adapted integrable reward process over a finite discrete horizon, the Snell envelope computes the conditional optimal reward by comparing immediate exercise with continuation.

Uniform-offer stopping recursion (vj​=(1+vj−12​)/2,v1​=1/2)

Words: 47
Optimal stopping OurBigBook.com
With independent uniform distributions on [0,1] as sequential offers and a finite number of rounds, the continuation value with j−1 offers remaining is vj−1​. Accept the current offer when it reaches that threshold. Integrating the maximum of the offer and continuation value gives the recursion, by the Snell envelope principle.

Smooth pasting

Words: 53
Optimal stopping OurBigBook.com
At a regular exercise boundary for a diffusion optimal stopping problem, value matching is commonly accompanied by matching first derivatives. This makes the value C1 across the boundary and eliminates a derivative-jump local time of a semimartingale term in the generalized Itô formula. It does not assert that second derivatives agree, or that smooth fit holds for every possible stopping problem.

Optimal stopping value function (V(t,s))

Words: 275 Articles: 2
Optimal stopping OurBigBook.com
For a Markov process with reward f, the value starting at time t in state s is the supremum of expected rewards over admissible stopping times. In finite discrete time it obeys V(T,s)=f(s) and V(t,s)=max{f(s),PV(t+1,⋅)(s)} for the transition operator P, wherever expectations are well-defined. Statewise absolute integrability of every remaining-horizon reward makes these values finite.
Convexity of a random-walk Snell value function (Wt​(x)=max{f(x),E[Wt+1​(x+ξ)]})
Words: 103
Optimal stopping value function OurBigBook.com
The transition operator of an additive random walk preserves convex functions: apply their convexity inequality to x+ξ and y+ξ, then integrate. The pointwise maximum of convex functions preserves convexity too, so induction proves convexity of the Snell envelope Bellman functions. Expectations are allowed to be extended-valued until finiteness is justified. Integrability of rewards on a finite horizon implies finiteness of these functions at every state for t≥1, by integrability of translated convex random-walk rewards and the bound Wt​(x)≤∑j=0T−t​E[f(x+Zj​)+]. At time zero only X0​=0 is observed; if W0​ is infinite elsewhere, its finite value at zero has a constant convex extension representing the same Snell envelope. Full statewise Bellman recursion at time zero requires an additional translated-integrability hypothesis.
Integrability of translated convex random-walk rewards
Words: 120
Optimal stopping value function OurBigBook.com
Let Zj​ be the sum of j independent identically distributed real increments. For a finite convex function f, integrability of f(Zj​) and f(Zj+1​) implies integrability of f(Zj​+x) for every fixed x. Its negative part is controlled by negative part of a finite convex function is Lipschitz. For x>0, if the increment law is unbounded above, take an independent increment η with p=P(η≥x)>0. On this event convexity gives f(Zj​+x)+≤f(Zj​)++f(Zj​+η)+, so the expectation is bounded by Ef(Zj​)++p−1Ef(Zj+1​)+. If increments are bounded above by M, use Zj​≤jM and bound the positive part by f(Zj​)++f(jM+x)+. For x<0, use the symmetric lower-tail argument. This supplies translated integrability without assuming integrable increments or a growth bound on f.

Optimal stopping time

Words: 34
Snell envelope OurBigBook.com
An optimal stopping time attains the supremum of the expected reward over an admissible class of stopping times. For a finite-horizon Snell envelope, the first time at which its value equals the current reward is optimal.

Complementarity for the Snell envelope compensator

Words: 19
Snell envelope OurBigBook.com
For the Doob compensator of a Snell envelope, (Vn​−Zn​)(An+1​−An​)=0: compensation grows only on the stopping region Vn​=Zn​.

Optimal stopping time from the compensator

Words: 28
Snell envelope OurBigBook.com
The first time the Snell-envelope compensator is about to become positive is an optimal stopping time; before it the martingale part equals both value and reward at stopping.

Doob's martingale inequality

Words: 40
Martingale OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative submartingale X, the maximal tail bound is λP(maxk≤n​Xk​≥λ)≤E[Xn​;maxk≤n​Xk​≥λ]. Applied to the absolute value of a martingale and integrated over λ, it gives the Doob Lp maximal inequality; at p=2 this is the Doob L2 maximal inequality.

Doob's martingale convergence theorems

Words: 40
Martingale OurBigBook.com
These are convergence results for martingales and submartingales under appropriate one-sided or absolute-integrability bounds. They distinguish almost-sure convergence from convergence in mean: uniform integrability gives the latter. The martingale convergence theorem stated for an L1-bounded martingale is one standard member of the family.
